clinicalPearls: The most common porphyria, resulting from deficient activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, the fifth enzyme of haem biosynthesis
Predominantly acquired (type I) with a normal gene, occurring when hepatic enzyme activity is inhibited; a familial (type II) form has an inherited UROD mutation
Presents as a chronic blistering photosensitivity with skin fragility, vesicles and bullae, milia, erosions and scarring on sun-exposed skin, especially the backs of the hands
Additional features include hypertrichosis (notably on the temples and cheeks), hyperpigmentation and, in some, sclerodermoid change
It is a purely cutaneous (non-acute) porphyria without neurovisceral attacks, as the accumulating porphyrins are photoreactive rather than neurotoxic precursors
Key susceptibility factors include hepatic iron overload (often with HFE haemochromatosis variants), hepatitis C, HIV, alcohol excess and oestrogen exposure
The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised urinary uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin with raised isocoproporphyrin in faeces
Management combines removal of contributory factors, iron reduction by venesection and low-dose antimalarial therapy, alongside sun protection
reference.pathophysiology: Porphyria cutanea tarda develops when hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity falls below a critical threshold, whether from acquired inhibition alone or on the background of an inherited mutation. The enzyme sequentially decarboxylates uroporphyrinogen, so its deficiency causes accumulation of highly carboxylated, water-soluble and photoreactive porphyrins, particularly uroporphyrin. Hepatic iron, oxidative stress and cofactors such as hepatitis C, alcohol and oestrogens generate an inhibitor of the enzyme. Circulating porphyrins deposit in the skin and, on ultraviolet and visible light exposure, generate reactive oxygen species that damage the dermo-epidermal junction, producing the characteristic fragility and blistering.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudoporphyria from drugs (e.g. NSAIDs, diuretics) or renal dialysis
Variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria with skin involvement
Bullous pemphigoid and other subepidermal blistering disorders
Polymorphic light eruption and other photodermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary porphyrins showing uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin excess
Faecal porphyrin analysis for isocoproporphyrin, characteristic of the condition
Plasma fluorescence scanning to support the porphyria diagnosis
Iron studies and ferritin, with HFE genotyping where iron overload is present
Hepatitis C and HIV serology, and assessment of alcohol intake and liver function
UROD gene testing when a familial form is suspected
redFlags: Features of advanced chronic liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma given the raised long-term risk
Severe childhood-onset blistering suggesting hepatoerythropoietic porphyria
Secondary infection or scarring of fragile skin lesions
Unrecognised underlying hepatitis C or HIV
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is good when contributory factors are addressed; skin lesions usually remit with iron reduction and antimalarial therapy, although there is a long-term risk of hepatic fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly with concurrent hepatitis C or alcohol excess.
pitfalls: Overlooking treatable drivers such as hepatitis C, HIV, alcohol, oestrogen use and iron overload
Confusing it with pseudoporphyria, which has identical skin changes but normal porphyrins
Failing to distinguish it from variegate porphyria, which can look identical on the skin
Neglecting sun protection while awaiting the effect of definitive treatment
Missing familial disease and the need for family assessment
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Iron depletion by repeated therapeutic venesection to reduce hepatic iron and relieve inhibition of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Low-dose antimalarial therapy with hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine to mobilise and clear accumulated hepatic porphyrins where venesection is unsuitable
Removal of susceptibility factors, including abstaining from alcohol, stopping oestrogen exposure, treating hepatitis C with direct-acting antivirals and optimising HIV therapy
Strict photoprotection with sun avoidance, protective clothing and barrier measures, plus gentle skin care to limit fragility and blistering
Monitoring of urinary porphyrins to confirm biochemical remission and of liver function with hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in those with cirrhosis or hepatitis C
Iron studies with HFE genotyping, and UROD gene testing with family assessment where a familial form is suspected
